claim: Self-assembly of ESCRT-III complex is a critical step in all ESCRT-dependent events.
source: Self-assembly of ESCRT-III complex is a critical step in all ESCRT-dependent events.
evidence: This is a general statement about ESCRT-III function that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: ESCRT-III hetero-polymers adopt variable architectures.
source: ESCRT-III hetero-polymers adopt variable architectures, but the mechanisms of inter-subunit recognition in these hetero-polymers to create flexible architectures remain unclear.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field and is referenced in the introduction section.

claim: The Saccharomyces cerevisiae ESCRT-III subunit Snf7 uses a conserved acidic helix to recruit its partner Vps24.
source: We demonstrate in vivo and in vitro that the Saccharomyces cerevisiae ESCRT-III subunit Snf7 uses a conserved acidic helix to recruit its partner Vps24.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental approaches described in the manuscript including in vivo and in vitro assays.

claim: Charge-inversion mutations in helix-4 of Snf7 inhibit Snf7-Vps24 lateral interactions in the polymer.
source: Charge-inversion mutations in this helix inhibit Snf7-Vps24 lateral interactions in the polymer, while rebalancing the charges rescues the functional defects.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from mutagenesis studies and functional assays shown in the manuscript.

claim: Rebalancing the charges in Snf7 helix-4 rescues the functional defects caused by charge-inversion mutations.
source: Charge-inversion mutations in this helix inhibit Snf7-Vps24 lateral interactions in the polymer, while rebalancing the charges rescues the functional defects.
evidence: This is demonstrated through genetic suppressor experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Snf7-Vps24 assembly occurs through electrostatic interactions on one surface, rather than through residue-to-residue specificity.
source: These data suggest that Snf7-Vps24 assembly occurs through electrostatic interactions on one surface, rather than through residue-to-residue specificity.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the charge-inversion and suppressor mutation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cooperative electrostatic interactions in the ESCRT-III polymer propagate to allow for specific inter-subunit recognition.
source: We propose a model in which these cooperative electrostatic interactions in the polymer propagate to allow for specific inter-subunit recognition, while sliding of laterally interacting polymers enable changes in architecture at distinct stages of vesicle biogenesis.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data and structural analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sliding of laterally interacting polymers enables changes in architecture at distinct stages of vesicle biogenesis.
source: We propose a model in which these cooperative electrostatic interactions in the polymer propagate to allow for specific inter-subunit recognition, while sliding of laterally interacting polymers enable changes in architecture at distinct stages of vesicle biogenesis.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental observations and structural considerations.

claim: ESCRTs drive biogenesis of multivesicular bodies (MVBs).
source: These include biogenesis of multivesicular bodies (MVBs) (Katzmann et al., 2001; Odorizzi et al., 1998), viral budding (Garrus et al., 2001), cytokinesis (Carlton and Martin-Serrano, 2007), nuclear envelope reformation (Olmos et al., 2015; Vietri et al., 2015), plasma membrane repair (Jimenez et al., 2014), surveillance of defective nuclear pore complexes (Webster et al., 2014), lysosomal protein degradation (Zhu et al., 2017), endolysosomal repair (Skowyra et al., 2018), and so on Hurley (2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ESCRTs drive viral budding.
source: These include biogenesis of multivesicular bodies (MVBs) (Katzmann et al., 2001; Odorizzi et al., 1998), viral budding (Garrus et al., 2001), cytokinesis (Carlton and Martin-Serrano, 2007), nuclear envelope reformation (Olmos et al., 2015; Vietri et al., 2015), plasma membrane repair (Jimenez et al., 2014), surveillance of defective nuclear pore complexes (Webster et al., 2014), lysosomal protein degradation (Zhu et al., 2017), endolysosomal repair (Skowyra et al., 2018), and so on Hurley (2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ESCRTs drive cytokinesis.
source: These include biogenesis of multivesicular bodies (MVBs) (Katzmann et al., 2001; Odorizzi et al., 1998), viral budding (Garrus et al., 2001), cytokinesis (Carlton and Martin-Serrano, 2007), nuclear envelope reformation (Olmos et al., 2015; Vietri et al., 2015), plasma membrane repair (Jimenez et al., 2014), surveillance of defective nuclear pore complexes (Webster et al., 2014), lysosomal protein degradation (Zhu et al., 2017), endolysosomal repair (Skowyra et al., 2018), and so on Hurley (2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ESCRTs drive nuclear envelope reformation.
source: These include biogenesis of multivesicular bodies (MVBs) (Katzmann et al., 2001; Odorizzi et al., 1998), viral budding (Garrus et al., 2001), cytokinesis (Carlton and Martin-Serrano, 2007), nuclear envelope reformation (Olmos et al., 2015; Vietri et al., 2015), plasma membrane repair (Jimenez et al., 2014), surveillance of defective nuclear pore complexes (Webster et al., 2014), lysosomal protein degradation (Zhu et al., 2017), endolysosomal repair (Skowyra et al., 2018), and so on Hurley (2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ESCRTs drive plasma membrane repair.
source: These include biogenesis of multivesicular bodies (MVBs) (Katzmann et al., 2001; Odorizzi et al., 1998), viral budding (Garrus et al., 2001), cytokinesis (Carlton and Martin-Serrano, 2007), nuclear envelope reformation (Olmos et al., 2015; Vietri et al., 2015), plasma membrane repair (Jimenez et al., 2014), surveillance of defective nuclear pore complexes (Webster et al., 2014), lysosomal protein degradation (Zhu et al., 2017), endolysosomal repair (Skowyra et al., 2018), and so on Hurley (2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ESCRTs drive surveillance of defective nuclear pore complexes.
source: These include biogenesis of multivesicular bodies (MVBs) (Katzmann et al., 2001; Odorizzi et al., 1998), viral budding (Garrus et al., 2001), cytokinesis (Carlton and Martin-Serrano, 2007), nuclear envelope reformation (Olmos et al., 2015; Vietri et al., 2015), plasma membrane repair (Jimenez et al., 2014), surveillance of defective nuclear pore complexes (Webster et al., 2014), lysosomal protein degradation (Zhu et al., 2017), endolysosomal repair (Skowyra et al., 2018), and so on Hurley (2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ESCRTs drive lysosomal protein degradation.
source: These include biogenesis of multivesicular bodies (MVBs) (Katzmann et al., 2001; Odorizzi et al., 1998), viral budding (Garrus et al., 2001), cytokinesis (Carlton and Martin-Serrano, 2007), nuclear envelope reformation (Olmos et al., 2015; Vietri et al., 2015), plasma membrane repair (Jimenez et al., 2014), surveillance of defective nuclear pore complexes (Webster et al., 2014), lysosomal protein degradation (Zhu et al., 2017), endolysosomal repair (Skowyra et al., 2018), and so on Hurley (2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ESCRTs drive endolysosomal repair.
source: These include biogenesis of multivesicular bodies (MVBs) (Katzmann et al., 2001; Odorizzi et al., 1998), viral budding (Garrus et al., 2001), cytokinesis (Carlton and Martin-Serrano, 2007), nuclear envelope reformation (Olmos et al., 2015; Vietri et al., 2015), plasma membrane repair (Jimenez et al., 2014), surveillance of defective nuclear pore complexes (Webster et al., 2014), lysosomal protein degradation (Zhu et al., 2017), endolysosomal repair (Skowyra et al., 2018), and so on Hurley (2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The ESCRT machinery consists of five evolutionarily conserved complexes: ESCRT-0, I, II, III and the AAA ATPase Vps4.
source: This machinery consists of five evolutionarily conserved complexes, ESCRT-0, I, II, III and the AAA ATPase Vps4.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: ESCRT-0, I and II are recruited to the membrane through interactions with ubiquitinated proteins.
source: ESCRT-0, I and II are recruited to the membrane through interactions with ubiquitinated proteins, while ESCRT-0 and ESCRT-II also bind phosphatidyl-inositol-3-phosphate (PI3P) at membranes (Robinson et al., 1988; Rothman et al., 1989; Raymond et al., 1992; Katzmann et al., 2001; Babst et al., 1997; Katzmann et al., 2003; Babst et al., 2002a; Babst et al., 2002b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ESCRT-0 and ESCRT-II bind phosphatidyl-inositol-3-phosphate (PI3P) at membranes.
source: ESCRT-0, I and II are recruited to the membrane through interactions with ubiquitinated proteins, while ESCRT-0 and ESCRT-II also bind phosphatidyl-inositol-3-phosphate (PI3P) at membranes (Robinson et al., 1988; Rothman et al., 1989; Raymond et al., 1992; Katzmann et al., 2001; Babst et al., 1997; Katzmann et al., 2003; Babst et al., 2002a; Babst et al., 2002b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ESCRT-II recruits ESCRT-III and nucleates ESCRT-III polymerization.
source: ESCRT-II recruits ESCRT-III, also nucleating ESCRT-III polymerization.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Polymerization of ESCRT-III is dynamically rearranged and directed towards disassembly via the recruitment of the AAA ATPase Vps4.
source: Polymerization of ESCRT-III is dynamically rearranged and directed towards disassembly via the recruitment of the AAA ATPase Vps4 (Mierzwa et al., 2017; Adell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ESCRT-III is ubiquitously required in all ESCRT-dependent processes.
source: ESCRT-III, however, is ubiquitously required in all ESCRT-dependent processes.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The membrane-modifying property of ESCRT-III is assumed to be a direct consequence of its self-assembly into meso-scale polymers.
source: This membrane-modifying property of ESCRT-III is assumed to be a direct consequence of its self-assembly into meso-scale polymers.
evidence: This is a general understanding in the field based on previous research.

claim: In yeast, the 'core' ESCRT-III machinery consists of Vps20, Snf7, Vps24 and Vps2.
source: In yeast, the 'core' ESCRT-III machinery consists of Vps20, Snf7, Vps24 and Vps2, as the deletion of any of these four genes leads to a strong defect in the MVB pathway (Babst et al., 2002b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Deletion of any of the core ESCRT-III genes (Vps20, Snf7, Vps24, Vps2) leads to a strong defect in the MVB pathway.
source: In yeast, the 'core' ESCRT-III machinery consists of Vps20, Snf7, Vps24 and Vps2, as the deletion of any of these four genes leads to a strong defect in the MVB pathway (Babst et al., 2002b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Other ESCRT-III proteins consist of Ist1, Did2, Vps60 and Chm7, which have accessory roles in the MVB pathway.
source: Other ESCRT-III proteins consist of Ist1, Did2, Vps60 and Chm7, which have accessory roles in the MVB pathway, but are essential in mammalian cytokinesis (Ist1/Did2) (Bajorek et al., 2009a) or nuclear envelope sealing (Chm7) (Webster et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ist1 and Did2 are essential in mammalian cytokinesis.
source: Other ESCRT-III proteins consist of Ist1, Did2, Vps60 and Chm7, which have accessory roles in the MVB pathway, but are essential in mammalian cytokinesis (Ist1/Did2) (Bajorek et al., 2009a) or nuclear envelope sealing (Chm7) (Webster et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Chm7 is essential in nuclear envelope sealing.
source: Other ESCRT-III proteins consist of Ist1, Did2, Vps60 and Chm7, which have accessory roles in the MVB pathway, but are essential in mammalian cytokinesis (Ist1/Did2) (Bajorek et al., 2009a) or nuclear envelope sealing (Chm7) (Webster et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: All ESCRT-III proteins consist of an N-terminal helical bundle, which is predominantly basic.
source: All ESCRT-III proteins consist of an N-terminal helical bundle, which is predominantly basic, and a C-terminal flexible and acidic region (Muzioł et al., 2006; Bajorek et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: All ESCRT-III proteins have a C-terminal flexible and acidic region.
source: All ESCRT-III proteins consist of an N-terminal helical bundle, which is predominantly basic, and a C-terminal flexible and acidic region (Muzioł et al., 2006; Bajorek et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The N-terminal helical bundle is important for ESCRT-III co-assembly.
source: The N-terminal helical bundle is known to be important for ESCRT-III co-assembly (Henne et al., 2012), while the C-terminus recruits the AAA ATPase Vps4 (Obita et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The C-terminus of ESCRT-III proteins recruits the AAA ATPase Vps4.
source: The N-terminal helical bundle is known to be important for ESCRT-III co-assembly (Henne et al., 2012), while the C-terminus recruits the AAA ATPase Vps4 (Obita et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Different architectures of ESCRT-III polymers have been visualized with electron microscopy including flat sheets, rings, spirals and helices.
source: Different architectures of ESCRT-III polymers have been visualized with electron microscopy – flat sheets, rings, spirals and helices, owing to the flexible nature of the polymers (Henne et al., 2012; Hanson et al., 2008; Chiaruttini et al., 2015; Shen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Snf7 forms 2D spirals.
source: The most abundant of the ESCRT-III proteins, Snf7, forms 2D spirals.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Combination of Snf7 with downstream proteins Vps24 and Vps2 changes the architecture of spirals to form three dimensional helical polymers.
source: Combination of Snf7 with downstream proteins Vps24 and Vps2 changes the architecture of these spirals to form three dimensional helical polymers (Henne et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The mammalian orthologues of Vps24 and Vps2 (CHMP3 and CHMP2) co-assemble to form helical structures.
source: The mammalian orthologues of Vps24 and Vps2 (named CHMP3 and CHMP2) co-assemble to form helical structures (Lata et al., 2008), whereas Vps24 has been visualized to form linear polymers (Ghazi-Tabatabai et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Vps24 has been visualized to form linear polymers.
source: The mammalian orthologues of Vps24 and Vps2 (named CHMP3 and CHMP2) co-assemble to form helical structures (Lata et al., 2008), whereas Vps24 has been visualized to form linear polymers (Ghazi-Tabatabai et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Helix-4 of Snf7 lies at the periphery of the core longitudinal interface.
source: Helix-4 of Snf7 lies at the periphery of this core longitudinal interface (Figure 1A–1B) and stretches from residue ~120 to~150.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Helix-4 of Snf7 stretches from residue ~120 to ~150.
source: Helix-4 of Snf7 lies at the periphery of this core longitudinal interface (Figure 1A–1B) and stretches from residue ~120 to~150.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of Snf7.

claim: In the crystal structure of Snf7core, residues D124 to E138 are structured.
source: In the crystal structure of Snf7core, which included residues 12–150, we observed that residues D124 to E138 are structured, while the rest of the amino acids are not visible.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure data.

claim: Helix-4 of Snf7 is mostly acidic in nature, with the acidic residues falling on one interface.
source: Helix-4 is mostly acidic in nature, with the acidic residues falling on one interface (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Deleting helix-4 of Snf7 results in a defect in recruiting Vps24-GFP to endosomes.
source: We had previously observed that deleting helix-4 of Snf7 resulted in a defect in recruiting Vps24-GFP to endosomes, although we did not have a mechanistic understanding behind this phenotype (Henne et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of CHMP1B depicts extensive electrostatic contacts made by CHMP1B's acidic residues of helices 4 and 5 with the basic helix-1 of IST1.
source: Interestingly, the previously solved cryo-EM structure of CHMP1B (which is the mammalian homolog of Did2) depicted extensive electrostatic contacts made by CHMP1B's acidic residues of helices 4 and 5 with the basic helix-1 of IST1 (McCullough et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous structural work.

claim: The overall acidity of Snf7 helix-4 is conserved in the Snf7 orthologues of multiple species.
source: The overall acidity of Snf7 helix-4 is conserved in the Snf7 orthologues of Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Homo sapiens, Mus musculus, Xenopus laevis, Drosophila melanogaster, Caenorhabditis elegans, and Schizosaccharomyces pombe (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), which suggests an important role of the electrostatics mediated by these charged residues.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mutations in the acidic residues of helix-4 have strong sensitivity to canavanine.
source: Using this canavanine-sensitivity assay, we found that mutations in the acidic residues of helix-4 have strong sensitivity to canavanine (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mutations in residues D131 and D127 show the strongest phenotype in canavanine sensitivity.
source: Mutations in residues D131 and D127 show the strongest phenotype (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Charge-inversion single mutations (D to K) or double-alanine (D127A D131A) mutations showed strong effects in cargo sorting.
source: Charge-inversion single mutations (D to K) or double-alanine (D127A D131A) mutations showed strong effects in cargo sorting, while single mutations to alanine do not show any defects (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Single mutations to alanine in helix-4 do not show any defects in cargo sorting.
source: Charge-inversion single mutations (D to K) or double-alanine (D127A D131A) mutations showed strong effects in cargo sorting, while single mutations to alanine do not show any defects (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mutations in residues D127, D131, E138 and E142 gave the strongest effects in Mup1-pHluorin sorting assays.
source: In our assays, we observed that mutations in residues D127, D131, E138 and E142 gave the strongest effects (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: D127, D131 and E138 lie on the same surface on the structure of helix-4.
source: Importantly, D127, D131 and E138 lie on the same surface on the structure of helix-4 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The effects of the helix-4 mutants are not due to the instability of the mutated proteins.
source: The effects of the helix-4 mutants that we have observed are not due to the instability of the mutated proteins.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro characterization experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The helix-4 mutant D131K (with R52E) is able to form polymers of Snf7.
source: The helix-4 mutant D131K (with R52E) is able to form polymers of Snf7 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The D131K mutant showed defects in its lateral interaction, as it preferentially makes thinner filaments.
source: One important exception here was that the D131K mutant showed defects in its lateral interaction, as it preferentially makes thinner filaments (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A -inset).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: A similar fraction (~50%) of Snf7 bound to liposomes with both Snf7R52E and Snf7 R52E D131K proteins.
source: A similar fraction (~50%) of Snf7 bound to liposomes with both Snf7R52E and Snf7 R52E D131K proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by liposome binding assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Both Snf7R52E and Snf7 R52E D131K proteins showed a similar size-exclusion chromatogram.
source: Furthermore, both proteins showed a similar size-exclusion chromatogram (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is supported by size-exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C.

claim: In the crystal lattice of Snf7core, the helix-4 residue D131 makes electrostatic contacts with helix-1 residues K21 and K25 in trans on a laterally interacting polymer strand.
source: In the crystal lattice of Snf7core, the helix-4 residue D131 makes electrostatic contacts with helix-1 residues K21 and K25 in trans on a laterally interacting polymer strand (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mutating K21 and K25 individually do not have any defect in cargo sorting.
source: In vivo, mutating K21 and K25 individually do not have any defect in cargo sorting, while the double mutation K21E K25E has a mild defect (~60% MVB function (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: The double mutation K21E K25E has a mild defect (~60% MVB function).
source: In vivo, mutating K21 and K25 individually do not have any defect in cargo sorting, while the double mutation K21E K25E has a mild defect (~60% MVB function (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: Helices 1–4 of Snf7 can recruit VPS24-GFP to endosomes.
source: First, we found that helices 1–4 of Snf7 can recruit VPS24-GFP to endosomes.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Deleting helix-4 or making specific mutations in helix-4 (D131K) reduced the recruitment of Vps24-GFP.
source: However, deleting helix-4 or making specific mutations in helix-4 (D131K) reduced the recruitment (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In subcellular fractionation experiments, the helix-4 mutant snf7D131K recruited ~5 fold lower amount of Vps24 than the wild-type protein in the P13 (endosome-enriched) fraction.
source: In subcellular fractionation experiments, the helix-4 mutant snf7D131K recruited ~5 fold lower amount of Vps24 than the wild-type protein in the P13 (endosome-enriched) fraction (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In co-immunoprecipitation experiments, the amount of Snf7D131K bound to Vps24 was reduced by >10 fold compared to wild-type.
source: Similarly, in co-immunoprecipitation experiments, the amount of Snf7D131K bound to Vps24 was reduced by >10 fold compared to wild-type (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In in vitro lipid monolayer assays, the Snf7R52E D131K mutant was unable to form 3D helical spirals with Vps24 and Vps2.
source: Furthermore, in in vitro lipid monolayer assays, the Snf7R52E D131K mutant was unable to form 3D helical spirals with Vps24 and Vps2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In cells lacking Vps24, Snf7 sediments to fractions containing higher percent glycerol, indicating formation of higher order polymers of Snf7.
source: We previously observed that in cells lacking Vps24, Snf7 sediments to fractions containing higher percent glycerol, indicating formation of higher order polymers of Snf7 (Teis et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In the helix-4 mutant snf7D131K strain, Snf7D131K protein sediments towards the bottom of the gradient, indicating that snf7D131K VPS24 phenocopies SNF7 vps24Δ.
source: In the helix-4 mutant snf7D131K strain, we observed a strikingly similar phenotype, as the Snf7D131K protein sediments towards the bottom of the gradient, indicating that snf7D131K VPS24 phenocopies SNF7 vps24Δ (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by glycerol gradient data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Random mutagenesis of Vps24 identified several mutations on the helix-1 surface of Vps24 (Q16E, K26E and K33E) that could rescue the defect of the Snf7 helix-4 mutation.
source: This selection approach identified several mutations on the helix-1 surface of Vps24 (Q16E, K26E and K33E of Vps24) that were canavanine resistant in the snf7D131K background.
evidence: This is supported by genetic selection data.

claim: Q16E mutation on Vps24 gave the strongest effect in suppressing the defect of snf7D131K, as ~70% of Mup1-pHluorin is sorted with the vps24Q16E mutation in the background of snf7D131K.
source: Of these, Q16E mutation on Vps24 gave the strongest effect in suppressing the defect of snf7D131K, as ~70% of Mup1-pHluorin is sorted with the vps24Q16E mutation in the background of snf7D131K (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Vps24 mutants Q16E and R19E suppress the defects of Snf7 mutations D127K and D142K.
source: Interestingly, Vps24 mutants Q16E and R19E additionally also suppress the defects of other Snf7 mutations D127K and D142K (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The expression levels of the Vps24 mutant proteins were similar to wild-type Vps24.
source: Importantly, the expression levels of the Vps24 mutant proteins were similar to wild-type Vps24 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The sulfhydryl crosslinker BMOE crosslinks Snf7D131C to cysteine mutations in helix-1 of Vps24 (Vps24Q16C, Vps24R19C and Vps24K26C).
source: Consistent with the idea that Snf7 helix-4 interacts with the helix-1 surface of Vps24, the sulfhydryl crosslinker BMOE crosslinks Snf7D131C to cysteine mutations in helix-1 of Vps24 (Vps24Q16C, Vps24R19C and Vps24K26C) (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by crosslinking data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Snf7D131C:Snf7D131C crosslinks occur probably due to the fact that Snf7 spirals are flexible enough to bend and form crosslinks through the longitudinal surface.
source: In these assays, we also see Snf7D131C:Snf7D131C crosslinks probably due to the fact that Snf7 spirals are flexible enough to bend and form crosslinks through the longitudinal surface (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the crosslinking data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: The amount of crosslinked Vps24 decreases with additional mutations in the vicinity of D131 in Snf7 that reduce Vps24 binding.
source: The amount of crosslinked Vps24 decreases with additional mutations in the vicinity of D131 in Snf7 that reduce Vps24 binding (adding the D127K and E142K mutations - Snf7 D131C D127K and Snf7 D131C D127K E142K) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by crosslinking data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: With the presence of D127K and E142K mutants, stronger Snf7-Snf7 crosslinking is observed, consistent with the observation that in the absence of Vps24, Snf7 forms higher amounts of polymers.
source: With the presence of these D127K and E142K mutants, we see stronger Snf7-Snf7 crosslinking, consistent with the observation that in the absence of Vps24, Snf7 forms higher amounts of polymers (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by crosslinking data and is consistent with previous observations.

claim: In the solved structure of CHMP1B-IST1, the helix-4 residues E106, S109 and D113 of CHMP1B are in close proximity to form salt bridges with IST1 helix-1 residues N14 and R16.
source: In the solved structure (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C), the helix-4 residues E106, S109 and D113 of CHMP1B are in close proximity to form salt bridges with IST1 helix-1 residues N14 and R16.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the CHMP1B-IST1 structure.

claim: The polar and acidic residues of helix-4 in CHMP1B and in Snf7 are conserved.
source: The polar and acidic residues of helix-4 in CHMP1B and in Snf7 are also conserved (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The IST1 structure is similar to the homology model of Vps24.
source: Additionally, the IST1 structure is similar to the homology model of Vps24 (using the hVps24 crystal structure as the template) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D) implying that the helix-1 residues probably are similarly positioned in a copolymer.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Error-prone mutagenesis with Snf7 identified several additional mutations in helix-4 of Snf7 that balanced the acidity of the helix and rescued the defect of the D131K mutation.
source: Through this genetic selection approach, we found that several additional mutations in helix-4 of Snf7 that balanced the acidity of the helix rescued the defect of the D131K mutation.
evidence: This is supported by genetic selection data.

claim: Charge-inversion double mutations D131K R134D and D131K R149D in the helix-4 region of Snf7 completely sort Mup1-pHluorin (~100%).
source: We found that charge-inversion double mutations D131K R134D and D131K R149D in the helix-4 region of Snf7 completely sorts Mup1-pHluorin (~100%), unlike the defective single mutant D131K (Figure 4A–4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-4B.

claim: The double mutant D127A D131A was rescued by the additional inclusion of the mutations R134D or R149D.
source: Additionally, the double mutant D127A D131A was also rescued by the additional inclusion of the mutations R134D or R149D (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C.

claim: Mutating the basic residue R134 or R149 to alanine rescued the defect of the D131K or the double-mutant D127A D131A.
source: Upon further analysis, to our surprise, mutating the basic residue R134 or R149 to alanine also rescued the defect of the D131K or the double-mutant D127A D131A (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mutating K125 to Glu in snf7D131K only partially suppressed the defect.
source: Mutating this Lys (K125) to Glu in snf7D131K only partially suppressed the defect (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), unlike the charge-inversion mutants of the same surface of the helix (R134, R149).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mutations in the polar amino acid Q136 to Glu on the opposite surface of the helix did not suppress the defect of snf7D131K.
source: Mutations in the polar amino acid Q136 to Glu on the opposite surface of the helix did not suppress the defect of snf7D131K (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mutations R134 to Glu, or R149 to Glu completely suppressed the defects of both D127K and E142K.
source: Mutations R134 to Glu, or R149 to Glu completely suppressed the defects of both D127K and E142K.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and 1D.

claim: Snf7 alone primarily forms flat spirals in vitro.
source: Snf7 alone primarily forms flat spirals in vitro (Henne et al., 2012; Chiaruttini et al., 2015; Shen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Overexpression of CHMP4, the mammalian homologue of Snf7, produces flat spirals or 3D helical structures in cells.
source: Overexpression of CHMP4, the mammalian homologue of Snf7 produces flat spirals or 3D helical structures in cells, that are similar to the spirals observed in vitro (Hanson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Incubating Snf7R52E, Vps24 and Vps2 on lipid monolayers produce architecturally distinct polymers similar to three-dimensional super-helical structures.
source: We previously observed that incubating Snf7R52E, Vps24 and Vps2 on lipid monolayers produce architecturally distinct polymers similar to three-dimensional super-helical structures (Henne et al., 2012), distinct from the flat, 2D spirals.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: At lower concentrations (1 μM each of Snf7R52E, Vps24 and Vps2) and shorter incubation times on lipid monolayers (10 min), all three proteins are required for the formation of 3D helices.
source: At lower concentrations (1 μM each of Snf7R52E, Vps24 and Vps2) and shorter incubation times on lipid monolayers (10 min), all three proteins are required for the formation of 3D helices (Figure 5—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1-2.

claim: At higher concentrations (7 μM of Snf7R52E) and shorter times (10 min), just Snf7R52E and Vps24 can together form 3D helices, albeit at a lower frequency.
source: However, at higher concentrations (7 μM of Snf7R52E) and shorter times (10 min), just Snf7R52E and Vps24 can together form 3D helices, albeit at a lower frequency (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and C.

claim: 3D helices of Snf7R52E alone are occasionally observed at higher concentrations (7 μM) and longer incubation times of 60 min, but these occur at a very low frequency.
source: We occasionally observe 3D helices of Snf7R52E alone at higher concentrations (7 μM) and longer incubation times of 60 min (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), but these occur at a very low frequency (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: Snf7 has an intrinsic flexibility to transform into 3D helices, which are accelerated by the addition of its partners Vps24/Vps2.
source: These data suggest that Snf7 has an intrinsic flexibility to transform into 3D helices, which are accelerated by the addition of its partners Vps24/Vps2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Pure filaments of Snf7 have an ability to form lateral interactions into bundles.
source: Pure filaments of Snf7 also have an ability to form lateral interactions into bundles, as we and others have observed before (Henne et al., 2012; Chiaruttini et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: At lower concentrations (500 nM) and shorter incubation time (10 min), Snf7R52E can form single stranded filaments.
source: At lower concentrations (500 nM) and shorter incubation time (10 min), Snf7R52E can form single stranded filaments (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: At higher concentrations (1 μM and above), Snf7R52E predominantly forms bundles through lateral interactions.
source: At higher concentrations (1 μM and above), this mutant predominantly forms bundles through lateral interactions (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: With wild-type Snf7 in the presence of Snf7's nucleator Vps20, predominantly single-stranded filaments of Snf7 (width of ~4–5 nm) are observed.
source: To observe the earlier stages of copolymer assembly, in our assays, we used wild-type Snf7 in the presence of Snf7's nucleator Vps20. With these assays, we observed predominantly single-stranded filaments of Snf7 (width of ~4–5 nm) (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5.

claim: With the addition of Vps24 and Vps2, thicker filaments were formed, suggesting that Vps24 and Vps2 induce formation of laterally-interacting polymers.
source: With the addition of Vps24 and Vps2, thicker filaments were formed, suggesting that Vps24 and Vps2 induce formation of laterally-interacting polymers, consistent with previous observations (Mierzwa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5 and is consistent with previous observations.

claim: The helix-4 mutant Snf7D131K is defective in inducing lateral bundles with Vps24/Vps2.
source: Importantly, the helix-4 mutant Snf7D131K is defective in inducing lateral bundles (Figure 5) with Vps24/Vps2, while the suppressor Vps24Q16E mutant forms a higher density of polymers and also partially rescues the bundling property.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The suppressor Vps24Q16E mutant forms a higher density of polymers and partially rescues the bundling property.
source: Importantly, the helix-4 mutant Snf7D131K is defective in inducing lateral bundles (Figure 5) with Vps24/Vps2, while the suppressor Vps24Q16E mutant forms a higher density of polymers and also partially rescues the bundling property.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The recruitment kinetics of ESCRT-III proteins Snf7, Vps24 and Vps2 is indistinguishable in vivo.
source: Recent evidence suggests that in vivo, the recruitment kinetics of ESCRT-III proteins Snf7, Vps24 and Vps2 is indistinguishable (Mierzwa et al., 2017; Adell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Overexpressing Vps24 or Vps2 by ~16 fold completely rescued the snf7D131K defect.
source: However, overexpressing Vps24 or Vps24 by ~16 fold (with a CMV promoter under a tet-off operator) completely rescued the snf7D131K defect (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Over-expressing Vps24 or Vps2 by ~2 fold did not rescue the defect of the Snf7 helix-4 mutant.
source: Over-expressing Vps24 or Vps2 by ~2 fold (using a CEN plasmid) did not rescue the defect of the Snf7 helix-4 mutant.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Overexpression of Vps24 or Vps2 increases the bound fraction of the Vps24/Vps2 complex in the Snf7D131K polymer, rescuing the defect of the mutant Snf7.
source: These analyses suggest that the overexpression of Vps24 or Vps2 increases the bound fraction of the Vps24/Vps2 complex in the Snf7D131K polymer, rescuing the defect of the mutant Snf7.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Overexpression of Vps24 or Vps2 did not rescue several longitudinal polymerization defective mutants of Snf7.
source: Consistent with this idea, overexpression of Vps24 or Vps2 did not rescue several longitudinal polymerization defective mutants of Snf7 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: Vps24 recognizes helix-4 in Snf7, which, along with Vps2, lies at the periphery of the core polymer, allowing for lateral association of these ESCRT-III proteins.
source: Altogether, our data provide strong evidence that Vps24 recognizes helix-4 in Snf7, which, along with Vps2, lies at the periphery of the core polymer, allowing for lateral association of these ESCRT-III proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The lateral interaction between Snf7 and Vps24 is mediated by promiscuous electrostatics, rather than specific residue-to-residue association.
source: This lateral interaction is mediated by promiscuous electrostatics, rather than specific residue-to-residue association.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.
